questions.explanation: The comparison needs the feature that explains approval and reliance, not merely a shared reservation category. The warning may change the result.

questions.stem: Rin read a notice conditioning fee-based events before payment. What reasoning bridge connects the disputed entry arrangements to reliance?
choices: Whether entry required payment determines whether the known approval condition applied to this event.
Whether entry required payment determines the nonrecoverable value of the printing expense.
Whether entry required payment determines whether the written booking identified the room and date.
Whether entry required payment determines the supply credit’s actual usability.
questions.explanation: The admission arrangement matters because it selects whether the warning qualified event approval. It does not directly establish unrelated facts or eliminate other elements.

questions.stem: Hale had a fully usable unrestricted credit; Rin has a one-year credit requiring a 100-dollar order. What follows from the difference?
choices: The full 60-dollar deposit is automatically lost whenever a credit expires someday.
The printing expense becomes unrecoverable because the supply vendor offered credit.
The full credit value is automatically usable because both cases contain the word credit.
Practical usability needs evidence; the restrictions alone do not establish a specific loss amount.
questions.explanation: The restrictions are legally relevant but do not prove their actual economic effect on this record. Analyze the expenses separately and seek usability facts.

questions.stem: Which sentence is an inference rather than a direct report of what F4 says?
choices: The approved payment wording suggests entrants may have been required to pay.
The proof contains the words "$5 at door."
The proof identifies Repair Circle, Room B and March 20.
Rin approved the proof on March 4.
questions.explanation: Saying the wording suggests required payment draws an inference. The other sentences directly describe the proof’s contents or its approval.

questions.stem: F5 establishes no refund, reuse or credit for Rin’s 90-dollar flyers. What limitation belongs in an analogy to reimbursed printing expenses?
choices: The comparison establishes that the supply deposit lacks any credit value.
The loss comparison supports value analysis, but Rin must still establish reasonable reliance.
The difference between 90 dollars and other case amounts bars any useful analogy.
The comparison proves the center never communicated an admission condition.
questions.explanation: A sound analogy on retained value does not decide every element. Different amounts do not erase the shared no-value rationale.

questions.stem: A paragraph says "Rin obtained manager approval" although the packet contains no such approval. What should the writer do?
choices: Cite Reed’s approval condition as proof of Rin’s manager approval.
Move the premise to a heading so it no longer requires factual support.
Remove the unsupported premise and state the record’s actual approval gap.
Keep the premise because it makes the application easier to follow.
questions.explanation: Application must use the actual record. A convenient invented fact cannot be repaired by relocation or a citation to another matter.

questions.stem: In a separate hypothetical, Dana has an unrestricted credit fully usable for an already planned purchase. Under § 4 and Hale, how should that payment be treated?
choices: It establishes that Rin also has a planned purchase, even though Rin’s record is silent.
It automatically proves reasonable reliance regardless of any approval condition.
It is a total loss solely because the vendor refused cash.
It retains recoverable value despite the lack of a cash refund.
questions.explanation: Dana’s supplied facts match Hale’s retained-value rationale. They do not alter Rin’s facts or settle a separate reliance issue.

questions.stem: Which comparison includes a legally significant reason rather than only a label?
choices: Rin and Hale both received credits, so the same full-value result follows without examining their terms.
Moss and Rin both bought flyers, so Rin need not separately establish reasonable reliance.
Unlike Hale’s fully usable credit, Rin’s minimum-order credit may require unwanted spending, so usability needs evidence.
Reed and Rin both received warnings, so the warnings must have the same effect regardless of applicability.
questions.explanation: The minimum-order comparison connects a credit restriction to practical recoverable value. The alternatives jump from a shared category to a result while skipping a material requirement or difference.

questions.stem: Match each comparison term to its meaning.
choices: Significant similarity
Significant difference
Conclusion from evidence
Starting fact or claim
questions.explanation: Analogy and distinction require legal significance; an inference follows from evidence, while a premise is a starting proposition that needs support.

questions.stem: Reasoning from a legally significant similarity to a prior case is an ___.
questions.explanation: An analogy explains why the similarity matters under the rule or rationale.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest supported objection to Rin’s reliance claim?
choices: The supply vendor offered a credit, which by itself establishes that reliance on the booking was unreasonable.
Reed involved a conditional booking, which means no written reservation can support reasonable reliance.
The approved payment wording suggests a fee-based event subject to a known, unsatisfied approval condition.
The center canceled after payment, which by itself proves the earlier reliance was unreasonable.
questions.explanation: The payment wording and notice connect record evidence to Reed’s approval-condition reasoning. The other objections lack a material supported premise.

questions.stem: Which response fairly addresses the approved "$5 at door" wording?
choices: Treat the client’s account as a judicial finding that conclusively defeats the proof.
Point to the optional-contribution note while acknowledging that the final entry arrangements remain unresolved.
Invent a later correction that the packet does not contain.
Declare the proof irrelevant because it is unfavorable to the client.
questions.explanation: A response should evaluate competing evidence and retain a real uncertainty. Ignoring adverse facts or inventing a correction does not answer the objection.

questions.stem: A memo predicts exactly a 73 percent chance of recovery based only on the packet. What is the problem?
choices: A prediction is forbidden whenever the case has any disputed fact.
A larger percentage would be justified because the client wants reimbursement.
Numerical odds become reliable if every case name is cited nearby.
The packet supplies no evidentiary basis for that numerical probability.
questions.explanation: Calibrate confidence through reasons and dependencies. No supplied data support a precise probability, though a reasoned qualitative prediction is appropriate.

questions.stem: What is the difference between F4’s payment wording and Reed’s approval-condition holding?
choices: F4 supplies adverse evidence about facts; Reed supplies potentially adverse legal authority.
Neither source can be discussed in an objective memorandum because it may hurt the claim.
F4 is binding law while Reed is an invoice establishing Rin’s payment amount.
Both sources conclusively establish the exact same event in Rin’s record.
questions.explanation: Evidence informs what happened; authority informs the legal consequence. Their roles differ, and both may be material to candid analysis.

questions.stem: Which conclusion properly separates Rin’s expenses?
choices: Neither expense can be analyzed until every imaginable fact is known.
The printing loss is documented but depends on reliance; the supply amount also depends on usable credit value.
The supply credit proves the separate printing expense has retained value.
Both payments were nonrefundable, so a 150-dollar award is certain.
questions.explanation: The expenses have different value evidence, while both still require reasonable reliance. A single unconditional total obscures those dependencies.

questions.stem: Which response to "the restrictions prove the credit is worthless" is best supported?
choices: The existence of any restriction makes Section 4 inapplicable.
The writer may assume a future purchase exists because that would make the answer definite.
Rin might be able to use a qualifying order; the record needs evidence about practical use before assigning loss.
Every restricted credit necessarily retains full face value regardless of its terms.
questions.explanation: A restriction does not prove zero value. Preserve the possible usefulness as an unresolved factual inquiry, without inventing a purchase or assuming full value.

questions.stem: Which issue has the clearest support on the supplied record: F5–F6 show March 5 payments and F7 shows March 7 cancellation, while entry and credit usability remain unresolved?
choices: Both payments occurred before cancellation.
The event unquestionably required payment for entry.
The organizer unquestionably satisfied reasonable reliance.
The supply credit unquestionably has no usable value.
questions.explanation: The dates establish timing. The other options erase express uncertainties about entry arrangements, value and resulting reliance.

questions.stem: A revised response concedes that mandatory admission would make Reed a strong obstacle. What effect should that have on a favorable prediction?
choices: Treat the concession as proof that mandatory admission actually occurred.
Remove all predictions because conceding any point makes analysis impossible.
Repeat the original unconditional conclusion without mentioning the concession.
Qualify the prediction by the unresolved admission premise and identify evidence that could resolve it.
questions.explanation: A candid concession can narrow a prediction. It does not establish the hypothetical premise or prevent a useful conditional assessment.

questions.stem: Match each counteranalysis component to its role.
choices: Unfavorable evidence
Contrary legal support
Evaluate objection
Calibrate confidence
questions.explanation: Counteranalysis distinguishes evidentiary and legal objections, evaluates them, and uses an appropriate qualifier for the supported prediction.

questions.stem: The process of testing a supported competing interpretation is ___.
questions.explanation: Counteranalysis evaluates the strongest supported objection and its effect on the prediction.

questions.stem: Which section should concisely state the outcome and its decisive qualifications?
choices: The statement of facts, with the prediction embedded as an established event.
The question presented, with the disputed premise already resolved in its wording.
The brief answer.
The memo header, with the outcome substituted for the subject description.
questions.explanation: The brief answer gives a reader the assessment and its main reasons. The header identifies the document, and supporting work products do not replace that summary.

questions.stem: Which facts sentence is neutral on this record?
choices: Rin’s note described optional contributions, while the approved proof stated "$5 at door."
The center’s fee-based label establishes the disputed entry arrangement conclusively.
Rin honestly planned free entry, and the center knowingly lied about the event.
The proof can be omitted because an objective writer should avoid contradictions.
questions.explanation: Attribute both supplied descriptions without unsupported judgments about honesty or intent. The contradiction is material and belongs in the factual account.

questions.stem: The discussion says credit usability is unknown, but the brief answer promises a 150-dollar award. What must change?
choices: Revise the summary to preserve the discussion’s uncertainty and separate expense assessments.
Delete the discussion’s support so it cannot contradict the promised amount.
Keep both because different sections may use different facts without explanation.
Move the guaranteed amount to the conclusion so it is no longer a summary.
questions.explanation: Internal consistency requires the brief answer and conclusion to reflect the actual reasoning, including unresolved reliance and credit value.

questions.stem: What is a practical reason to draft or revise the brief answer after developing the discussion?
choices: A late summary automatically resolves every factual dispute in the packet.
The summary can reflect the analysis and qualifications actually supported by the completed reasoning.
The order makes citations unnecessary in the rest of the memorandum.
Writing the summary last permits unsupported facts to be added without review.
questions.explanation: Drafting sequence can help align summary and reasoning. It does not remove the need for support or resolve missing facts by itself.

questions.stem: The assignment is an objective memo about KCRA reimbursement. Which conclusion supplies useful next steps?
choices: Recommend an unrelated legal theory without examining its governing law.
Promise full reimbursement because a concrete total sounds useful to the reader.
State only "more work is needed" without identifying any material question.
Seek final publicity and entry instructions, and investigate practical use of the restricted credit.
questions.explanation: The specified inquiries address the two material uncertainties. Useful next steps connect evidence requests to the prediction they could change.

questions.stem: How is the extended memorandum assignment completed in this course?
choices: Selecting the course awards university credit for the memorandum.
Finishing any quiz automatically submits the memo to a university instructor.
The app automatically grades the legal merits of an essay that has not been submitted.
Write it in your own document or notes and use the supplied model and rubric for self-assessment.
questions.explanation: The course provides a separate writing exercise, model and rubric. It does not collect or automatically grade the memorandum or award university credit.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly treats planning time and expected contributions under the supplied assignment?
choices: They should replace the printing expense because anticipated revenue is simpler to calculate.
They are outside the Act’s qualifying preparation-expense remedy; other legal claims remain outside scope.
Their exclusion proves that no legal claim under any other law could ever exist.
They are included whenever the organizer has a confirmed reservation.
questions.explanation: Section 5 limits this remedy, while the assignment does not resolve other claims. Do not expand an exclusion beyond its source.

questions.stem: A facts section states "communications occurred" but omits the approval notice and conflicting entry descriptions. What is the defect?
choices: A facts section must argue for the client rather than give useful factual detail.
Every communication must be reproduced verbatim regardless of relevance.
It lacks material detail needed to understand the dispute even if the vague sentence is technically true.
A neutral facts section cannot mention any evidence that points in competing directions.
questions.explanation: Neutrality requires accurate, material detail. Vague truth is insufficient when the omitted communications determine the central reliance issue.

questions.stem: Match each memo section to its reader function.
choices: Frame the dispute
Summarize prediction
Describe relevant record
Develop legal analysis
questions.explanation: The sections work together but serve distinct functions: question, assessment, record and developed reasoning.

questions.stem: The memo section giving a concise prediction and its principal qualifications is the ___ answer.
questions.explanation: The brief answer, also called a short answer, must match the discussion’s degree of confidence.

questions.stem: What does a reverse outline record?
choices: The function each paragraph in the existing draft actually performs.
Only the headings planned before any drafting began.
The desired result without checking the discussion’s organization.
A list of every punctuation mark changed during proofreading.
questions.explanation: A reverse outline maps the document as written, exposing gaps and repetition that the original plan may not reveal.

questions.stem: Which change is substantive revision rather than only line editing?
choices: Change one comma while leaving the same unsupported legal proposition intact.
Replace an unconditional 150-dollar award with separate assessments tied to reliance and credit value.
Adjust paragraph spacing without changing analytical relationships.
Replace a font while leaving all facts, rules and predictions unchanged.
questions.explanation: Separating the expenses and qualifying the prediction corrects the reasoning. Punctuation, spacing or font changes alone do not repair the unsupported award.

questions.stem: A draft says Rin paid 80 dollars for flyers. F5 says 90 dollars; Moss paid 80. What should a source audit do?
choices: Keep 80 dollars because that amount appears somewhere in the authority packet.
Remove F5 from the record so it no longer conflicts with the draft.
Average the two amounts because both sources discuss printing.
Correct the client amount to 90 dollars and check summaries for the same cross-record error.
questions.explanation: Source identity matters. Moss’s facts do not establish Rin’s amount, and a correction must reach every dependent section.

questions.stem: A revised discussion recognizes an unresolved credit value, but the old guaranteed total remains in the conclusion. What is needed?
choices: Leave the conclusion because the reader should prefer whichever section is newer.
Delete the credit’s actual restrictions to restore the original guaranteed result.
Update dependent sections so the final document states a consistent prediction.
Treat the contradiction as useful evidence that two outcomes are equally certain.
questions.explanation: Substantive revisions often propagate across the document. The conclusion must follow the revised reasoning rather than preserve a superseded prediction.

questions.stem: Which revision-log entry is sufficiently informative?
choices: Reviewed everything and concluded that it felt correct.
Made the paragraph look more professional.
Improved the memo in various unspecified ways.
Changed "any credit bars recovery" to a usable-value inquiry, citing § 4 and Hale ¶ 5’s reserved issue.
questions.explanation: A useful entry identifies the old claim, new claim, supporting source and analytical improvement. General impressions do not document a substantive revision.

questions.stem: The model uses a different confidence qualifier from a student’s memo. How should self-assessment proceed?
choices: Assume any different prediction earns full credit without checking sources.
Copy the model and describe it as the original first draft.
Compare the reasons, factual support and preserved uncertainties rather than demand identical wording.
Mark every different sentence incorrect regardless of its supporting analysis.
questions.explanation: A supported degree of confidence may differ, but the record and source limits must remain accurate. The model is an analytical example, not an exclusive script.

questions.stem: Which audit entry best distinguishes prediction from source description?
choices: State the predicted result, then identify the legal and factual premises that support that inference.
Omit all citations because predictions never depend on sources.
Treat the writer’s conclusion as a quotation from Hale without checking the opinion.
Search for a packet sentence that literally predicts Rin’s result and invent one if absent.
questions.explanation: A prediction is the writer’s inference. Audit its premises and reasoning instead of falsely attributing the final prediction to a source.

questions.stem: Which set matches the capstone workbench deliverables?
choices: Only a completed multiple-choice quiz and an assumed automatic essay grade.
Evidence matrix, first draft, revised memo, substantive revision log and source audit.
Only a case list without facts, discussion or a prediction.
Only a polished conclusion without the analysis on which it depends.
questions.explanation: The capstone makes drafting and revision visible through the listed work products. Quizzes test component skills but do not replace the memorandum.

questions.stem: Match each revision tool to its purpose.
choices: Map paragraph functions
Verify support
Explain changes
Improve sentence clarity
questions.explanation: These tools address organization, accuracy, documented changes and prose. Sentence editing alone does not validate the reasoning.

questions.stem: An outline made from the paragraph functions of an already written draft is a ___ outline.
questions.explanation: A reverse outline examines the document as written rather than merely repeating the original plan.

decks.title: Legal Writing I: Objective Analysis notecards

cards.front: What does an objective memo give its reader?
cards.back: A candid prediction with the supporting law, material facts, strongest contrary analysis and important uncertainties.

cards.front: How does a legal issue differ from a broad topic?
cards.back: An issue connects a decision and governing law to material facts. “Room cancellation” is a topic; reimbursement despite an approval condition and credit is an issue.

cards.front: Why is the entry-payment arrangement material for Rin?
cards.back: It determines whether F2’s fee-based approval condition applied before payment. F3 and F4 support competing inferences.

cards.front: What is established by F7’s cancellation label?
cards.back: The center described the event as fee-based and canceled it. The label does not conclusively establish what entrants would have had to pay.

cards.front: What should an evidence-matrix row contain?
cards.back: The requirement or question, legal source, favorable and adverse record facts, missing evidence and the provisional analytical consequence.

cards.front: How should an assumption about free entry be used?
cards.back: Label it as provisional, explain that branch’s result, and analyze the material alternative that payment was required.

cards.front: What is a useful follow-up about the supply deposit?
cards.back: Seek evidence of practical credit use, such as future qualifying purchases and transfer rights, because § 4 concerns recoverable value.

cards.front: Does excluding planning time under § 5 resolve all other legal remedies?
cards.back: No. It resolves the Act’s remedy within this assignment; unexamined claims under other law remain outside scope.

cards.front: What are the KCRA § 2 requirements?
cards.back: Covered reservation, center cancellation, reasonable reliance, and a nonrecoverable preparation expense paid before cancellation. Analyze each expense separately.

cards.front: How do an element and a factor differ here?
cards.back: Reasonable reliance is required; confirmation specificity, relevant prepayment warnings and event connection are considerations for evaluating it under § 3.

cards.front: What distinction reconciles Moss and Reed?
cards.back: Moss’s notice concerned room reassignment; Reed’s known, applicable condition left event approval pending before payment.

cards.front: What does Hale establish about a denied refund?
cards.back: No cash refund does not establish a loss if usable credit preserves the value. Hale’s full credit was usable for planned purchases.

cards.front: What does Hale leave unresolved?
cards.back: The treatment and valuation of restricted credits. Section 4 still requires evidence about actual recoverable value.

cards.front: Why is Hale not a holding resolving Rin’s disputed reliance?
cards.back: Reasonable reliance was conceded in Hale. Its decided question concerned retained value, so that concession does not decide Rin’s contested premise.

cards.front: What should a rule synthesis preserve?
cards.back: Statutory requirements, relevant case reasoning, factual conditions and express limits. It should explain relationships rather than count outcomes.

cards.front: Why is “printing always qualifies” an overstatement?
cards.back: A printing expense still must satisfy every § 2 requirement, including reasonable reliance and payment timing, as well as lack of recoverable value.

cards.front: Expand IRAC.
cards.back: Issue, rule, application, conclusion. The labels expose a reasoning sequence but do not supply missing analysis.

cards.front: Expand CREAC.
cards.back: Conclusion, rule, explanation, application, conclusion. Complex questions may require several paragraphs rather than five sentences.

cards.front: What belongs in explanation rather than application?
cards.back: What the authorities decided and why, using their relevant facts. Rin’s comparisons belong in application.

cards.front: Why organize by reliance and value instead of case names?
cards.back: The reader needs answers to legal questions. Multiple authorities can explain one question, and one authority can inform more than one analytical unit.

cards.front: What makes a point heading useful?
cards.back: It identifies an issue or supported proposition, such as reliance turning on whether entry required payment, without promising an unsupported result.

cards.front: What must a roadmap match?
cards.back: The final discussion’s actual order and questions. Update it when the organization changes.

cards.front: How much space should clear requirements receive?
cards.back: Enough to show they were considered and why they are met. Reserve fuller explanation for disputed requirements needing reasoning.

cards.front: What should a unit’s closing conclusion do?
cards.back: State the result supported by the preceding rule, explanation and application, preserving uncertainty without introducing a new unsupported premise.

cards.front: What are the core parts of a case illustration?
cards.back: Relevant facts, holding and reasoning, selected to explain the proposition the paragraph addresses.

cards.front: Which Moss facts matter to the warning comparison?
cards.back: A specific confirmation, a notice limited to room reassignment, no approval condition and an event-connected printing expense.

cards.front: Which Reed facts explain denial?
cards.back: An applicable safety-approval condition was known before payment and remained unsatisfied; the reservation heading did not erase it.

cards.front: How did Hale treat its two expenses?
cards.back: It denied the supplies covered by a fully usable unrestricted credit and allowed the separate 40-dollar nonrecoverable label expense.

cards.front: What does a pinpoint citation add?
cards.back: A precise route to the supporting paragraph or section, enabling the reader to verify the particular proposition rather than merely its topic.

cards.front: What makes a paraphrase inaccurate even when its topic is right?
cards.back: Dropping or changing a material qualification, such as prepayment knowledge, can broaden the claim beyond the source.

cards.front: When should wording be placed in quotation marks?
cards.back: When reproducing the source’s actual words. Check them exactly; do not label a loose paraphrase as a quotation.

cards.front: Can a correct citation format cure an unsupported proposition?
cards.back: No. Source identity, location and proposition fit must all be accurate. Revise the claim if the cited passage does not support it.

cards.front: What four parts make a comparison useful?
cards.back: Present fact, precedent fact, legally significant relationship, and consequence for the issue.

cards.front: Why is “both received warnings” incomplete?
cards.back: Moss and Reed show that a warning’s subject, applicability and timing matter. The shared label does not establish its legal effect.

cards.front: What is the reasoning bridge for Rin’s entry dispute?
cards.back: The entry arrangement determines whether the known fee-based approval condition qualified the confirmation before the expenses were paid.

cards.front: What inference can F4 support?
cards.back: Its approved “$5 at door” wording suggests required payment, but the competing optional-contribution account prevents treating that inference as conclusively established.

cards.front: What distinguishes Rin’s credit from Hale’s?
cards.back: A one-year expiration and a 100-dollar minimum order, with no supplied evidence of practical usability. Those differences justify inquiry, not an assumed loss amount.

cards.front: Why do different printing amounts not defeat the value analogy?
cards.back: The relevant feature is absence of refund, reuse or credit. Rin’s 90-dollar amount differs from precedent amounts without changing that feature.

cards.front: What remains after a successful printing-loss comparison?
cards.back: Rin still must establish reasonable reliance and the other § 2 requirements; one element’s analogy does not decide the entire claim.

cards.front: How should a transfer example be kept separate?
cards.back: Use its expressly supplied facts only for that hypothetical. Dana’s planned purchases do not become evidence that Rin has a usable credit.

cards.front: What is the strongest reliance objection in Rin’s record?
cards.back: The approved payment wording suggests a fee-based event, Rin knew the prepayment approval notice, and no required approval appears if that condition applied.

cards.front: What is the supported response to that objection?
cards.back: The free-entry confirmation and optional-contribution note support a different arrangement, but do not conclusively resolve the conflict with the proof.

cards.front: How do adverse evidence and adverse authority differ?
cards.back: Evidence bears on what happened; authority supplies the legal principle or comparison. F4 and Reed perform those different roles.

cards.front: Does a fair response have to eliminate all uncertainty?
cards.back: No. It may concede a material point and narrow the prediction while identifying evidence that could resolve the remaining premise.

cards.front: Why avoid a precise percentage chance of recovery here?
cards.back: The packet provides no data supporting numerical odds. Explain confidence through concrete reasons and dependencies instead.

cards.front: How should confidence differ across Rin’s expenses?
cards.back: Printing loss is documented but depends on reliance. The supply claim has the additional uncertainty of usable credit value.

cards.front: Why is “no recovery because a credit exists” overbroad?
cards.back: The credit concerns only supplies, its practical value is unresolved, and the separate printing expense has no credit. Hale supports separate expense analysis.

cards.front: What should an unresolved issue statement identify?
cards.back: The exact open question, why the available record or authority does not settle it, its effect on the prediction and the evidence that would help.

cards.front: What belongs in the question presented?
cards.back: The bounded legal question and material facts that make the dispute understandable, without resolving disputed premises silently.

cards.front: What belongs in the brief answer?
cards.back: A concise prediction, principal reasons and decisive qualifications consistent with the developed discussion.

cards.front: How do you present F3 and F4 neutrally?
cards.back: Attribute the note’s optional-contribution account and the proof’s payment wording, then identify the unresolved entry arrangement without unsupported honesty judgments.

cards.front: Why draft or revise the brief answer after discussion?
cards.back: It helps the summary reflect the analysis actually supported rather than an early assumption that later reasoning changed.

cards.front: What is the memo’s scope here?
cards.back: KCRA reimbursement on the fictional packet, including the § 5 exclusion. Other legal theories are unexamined rather than adjudged meritless.

cards.front: What reveals internal inconsistency?
cards.back: For example, the discussion leaves credit value open while the brief answer promises a guaranteed 150-dollar award.

cards.front: What concrete next steps belong in the conclusion?
cards.back: Obtain final publicity or entry instructions and investigate practical credit use, explaining how those facts could change reliance or the recoverable amount.

cards.front: Where is the extended memo completed and assessed?
cards.back: In the learner’s own document or notes, using the model and rubric for self-assessment. Quiz completion does not submit or automatically grade the memo.

cards.front: What does a reverse outline reveal?
cards.back: What each written paragraph actually does, including repetition, missing application and paragraphs with unrelated functions.

cards.front: What should be revised before sentence polish?
cards.back: Scope, structure, rule accuracy, factual support, application and counteranalysis. A polished sentence can still contain a substantive error.

cards.front: What should a proposition-source ledger record?
cards.back: The draft claim, precise locator, source’s actual support and limitations, and any needed correction.

cards.front: How do you audit a prediction rather than a quoted rule?
cards.back: Check its legal and factual premises and the inference connecting them. Do not attribute the writer’s prediction to a source that never stated it.

cards.front: What cross-record amount error should be caught?
cards.back: Moss paid 80 dollars for flyers; Rin paid 90. Use F5 for Rin and update dependent summaries if the wrong amount spread.

cards.front: What makes a revision-log entry substantive?
cards.back: It identifies the old claim, the corrected claim, the supporting source and why the change improves analysis, rather than merely noting formatting edits.

cards.front: How should the model memo be used?
cards.back: Read it after the first draft, compare reasoning and source limits, and use the rubric. Supported differences in confidence are possible; identical wording is unnecessary.

cards.front: What are the capstone deliverables?
cards.back: An evidence matrix, first draft, revised 900–1,100-word memo, at least three substantive revision entries and a source audit as specified in the workbench.

glossary.definition: A document that explains a legal problem and gives a candid, supported prediction, including material uncertainty and contrary evidence.
The defined legal, factual and product boundaries of the work requested.
A bounded legal question connected to facts that make the decision disputed.
A fact whose change could affect a legal requirement, inference or amount.
An unresolved question about what happened or what the available evidence establishes.
An unresolved question about a rule’s meaning or its application to a problem.
A labeled provisional premise used for analysis rather than treated as established evidence.
An expression of a legal requirement or standard that preserves its material conditions and limits.
A required component of a legal test.
A consideration used to evaluate a legal standard, rather than necessarily a separate absolute requirement.
Combining relevant legal propositions into a coherent account while preserving their conditions and differences.
The court’s decision of a legal issue necessary to its result on the facts before it.
A judicial observation beyond what is necessary to resolve the issue before the court.
An issue that an authority expressly leaves undecided.
An organizing sequence of issue, rule, application and conclusion.
An organizing sequence of conclusion, rule, explanation, application and conclusion.
Development of what relevant authorities establish and illustrate before applying them to the client’s record.
Analysis connecting the governing rule and authorities to the client’s facts.
A preview of the discussion’s analytical order that matches the organization actually used.
A coherent treatment of one legal question or requirement ending in a supported result for that question.
A heading identifying an issue or a supported analytical proposition.
A focused explanation of a legal proposition through a decision’s relevant facts, holding and reasoning.
Facts that matter to the legal reasoning on the proposition being discussed.
The reason supporting a legal decision or proposition.
A claim that a sentence or passage asks the reader to accept.
A citation identifying the precise source section, paragraph or other location supporting a proposition.
A restatement in the writer’s own words that preserves the source’s substance and material limitations.
An exact reproduction of source language, identified as quoted words.
Reasoning from a legally significant similarity between the present problem and a prior example.
An explanation of why a difference matters under the governing rule or rationale.
A conclusion drawn from evidence rather than directly stated by it.
The explanation connecting compared facts to their significance under the legal rule.
A fact on which an analytical conclusion depends and whose support must be checked.
Analysis of explicitly stated factual possibilities that can materially change the result.
A feature selected for comparison because the governing rule or rationale makes it significant.
Examination and evaluation of a supported competing interpretation and its effect on a prediction.
Evidence supporting an inference unfavorable to a tentative conclusion.
Legal authority supplying a principle or comparison that could support a contrary result.
An evaluation of an objection through law and evidence, which may distinguish, concede or narrow the prediction.
A reasoned assessment of the likely legal result on the supplied law and facts.
Language indicating the degree or condition of support for a prediction.
A question that remains open after analysis of the available materials, with its significance and limits identified.
The memo’s statement of the bounded legal question with material facts giving context to the dispute.
A concise prediction with its principal reasons and qualifications, consistent with the discussion.
A neutral account of relevant background and evidence needed to understand the analysis.
The memorandum section developing the governing law, application, counteranalysis and supported conclusions.
Accurate presentation of the record without loaded labels or conversion of disputed inferences into established facts.
A statement identifying the legal and factual boundaries of a document’s analysis.
Agreement across sections about facts, rules and the degree of confidence supported by the analysis.
An outline of the functions performed by paragraphs in an already written draft.
Revision improving analysis, organization or support rather than only surface expression.
Sentence-level revision for clarity, grammar and expression.
Verification of material propositions against the actual supporting legal and factual sources.
A record connecting draft claims to precise source support, limitations and needed revisions.
Correct source identity and location together with a genuine fit between the source and the cited proposition.
A record of changes explaining the old claim, revised claim, supporting source and analytical improvement.

references.title: Kestrel authority packet
references.body:
These are original fictional materials created for this course. They are not accounts of real statutes or decisions. Use the text below as the complete legal universe for the writing assignment. No outside research is required. The hypothetical forum is a Kestrel trial court. The three Court of Appeals opinions are binding in that forum on the issues they decide. None has been overruled in this teaching universe. The opinions apply the same version of the statute reproduced here; their dates do not imply different statutory versions. A question left open by an opinion remains open in the packet.

Use citations such as “KCRA § 3,” “Moss ¶ 4,” and “Hale ¶ 5.” These are packet locators, not representations of a real citation system. Cite the client record separately as F1–F7. Cite quoted words exactly; a paraphrase must preserve the source's conditions and limitations. Numbered paragraphs below are stable locators.

## Kestrel Community Room Act (KCRA)

### Section 1 — Covered reservation

A covered reservation is a community-center booking identified by event, room and date in a written confirmation sent by the center to the organizer. A confirmation may state a condition of approval. The existence of a covered reservation does not itself establish that reliance on it was reasonable.

### Section 2 — Reimbursement requirements

An organizer may recover a preparation expense if the organizer establishes all of the following: a covered reservation; cancellation of that reservation by the center; reasonable reliance on the reservation when incurring the expense; and a nonrecoverable preparation expense paid before the center's cancellation. Satisfaction of one requirement does not substitute for another. Analyze each claimed expense separately.

### Section 3 — Reasonable reliance

In deciding whether reliance was reasonable, consider the specificity of the center's confirmation, any relevant warning communicated to the organizer before payment, and the connection between the expense and the booked event. A warning is relevant to the extent that it concerns a condition applicable to that event or otherwise qualifies the commitment on which the organizer relied. No one factor automatically decides every case.

### Section 4 — Recoverable value

An expense is nonrecoverable to the extent that the organizer cannot obtain a refund, reuse the purchased item, or use an available vendor credit to recover its value. A separately identifiable nonrecoverable portion may qualify even when another portion retains value. The organizer must establish the amount that is nonrecoverable. The existence of a vendor credit requires inquiry into whether and to what extent it can actually recover value; its label alone does not settle that question.

### Section 5 — Scope of this remedy

Only qualifying preparation expenses are recoverable under this Act. Anticipated profit, the organizer's time, and inconvenience are excluded from this remedy. This Act and packet do not resolve possible claims under other law.

## Moss v. Civic Center (Kestrel Court of Appeals, 2022)

**¶ 1.** Moss received a written confirmation naming a community workshop, room and date. A footer stated that room assignments might change. The document contained no approval condition. Moss then paid 80 dollars for printed flyers naming that room and date. The center canceled the reservation before the workshop.

**¶ 2.** The parties agreed that the flyers were not refundable or reusable and that the expense was paid before cancellation. They disputed whether the footer made reliance unreasonable under KCRA § 3. The trial court denied reimbursement solely because the footer warned of possible changes.

**¶ 3.** The specificity of the confirmation and the warning's subject must be considered together. A notice about room reassignment does not, without more, communicate that the event itself awaits approval. The flyers were directly connected to the event identified in the confirmation.

**¶ 4.** Moss reasonably relied on the confirmation for this printing expense. The general room-reassignment notice did not withdraw or condition approval of the event. The court reversed the denial and directed reimbursement of 80 dollars under §§ 2–4.

**¶ 5.** The court did not decide the effect of a specific, applicable approval condition communicated before payment. Its decision addresses the notice and expense in this record, not every kind of warning or every preparation cost.

## Reed v. Civic Center (Kestrel Court of Appeals, 2023)

**¶ 1.** Reed received a writing headed “Reservation” that named a performance, room and date. The body expressly stated that approval depended on the manager's safety review. Reed acknowledged the condition by email before paying a nonrefundable equipment deposit. The manager had not approved the event when Reed paid.

**¶ 2.** The center later canceled the booking. Reed sought the deposit under KCRA § 2, arguing that the heading and named room created a sufficiently definite commitment. The parties did not dispute that the expense was connected to the performance and had been paid before cancellation.

**¶ 3.** The writing met § 1's identification requirements, but that did not settle § 3. The specific, applicable condition communicated before payment made reliance on final approval unreasonable on this record. The heading could not erase the express condition in the body.

**¶ 4.** The court affirmed denial of reimbursement because the reasonable-reliance requirement was not established. A nonrefundable expenditure does not itself prove reasonable reliance. The court distinguished Moss: its warning concerned a possible room change, not pending approval of the event.

**¶ 5.** The court did not hold that every warning defeats reasonable reliance. Its decision concerns an applicable approval condition known before payment and still unsatisfied when the expense was incurred. It did not decide a warning delivered only after payment or a condition unrelated to the event.

## Hale v. Civic Center (Kestrel Court of Appeals, 2024)

**¶ 1.** Hale received an unconditional written confirmation for a community meeting and reasonably relied on it. Before the center canceled, Hale paid a vendor 100 dollars for supplies and paid a printer 40 dollars for date-specific labels. All requirements other than nonrecoverable value were conceded.

**¶ 2.** The supply vendor denied a cash refund but provided an unrestricted credit for the full 100 dollars. The credit had no expiration or minimum order, and the record established that Hale could use its entire value for already planned purchases. The labels were nonrefundable, could not be reused, and carried no credit.

**¶ 3.** Section 4 concerns recoverable value, not only recovery in cash. Because Hale could use the credit's full value, the supply payment was not a nonrecoverable expense. Calling the payment a deposit and showing a denied refund did not change that result.

**¶ 4.** The court allowed the separate 40-dollar label expense and denied the 100-dollar supply claim. The two expenses required separate analysis; retained value in one did not defeat reimbursement of a distinct qualifying loss in the other.

**¶ 5.** The court expressly reserved credits with expiration dates, minimum orders, transfer restrictions, or other limitations affecting practical use. It did not prescribe a valuation formula for restricted credits. Such a claim requires evidence about available value under § 4; the presence or absence of full value cannot be assumed from this opinion alone.

## Reading boundaries

Moss and Reed can be read together because their warnings differ in legal significance. Hale addresses recoverable value on a record where reasonable reliance was conceded. Do not turn that concession into a holding about how reliance should be decided. Do not treat Hale's reserved issue as either a categorical exception or a categorical bar. For this assignment, explain the gap, apply § 4, identify facts that would matter, and make a conditional prediction. External sources are optional background for writing skills, never additional Kestrel authority.

references.title: Rin Patel client record
references.body:
All dates below fall in the same fictional year, after all three packet opinions. The planned event date is March 20. The writing assignment takes place on March 10, after cancellation but before the planned event. These seven items are the complete available record. Do not invent interviews, publicity, communications, invoices, approval or actual attendance. “Not established” means absent from this record, not proven false.

## F1 — March 2 confirmation

The Kestrel Civic Center emailed Rin Patel: “Confirmed: Repair Circle, Room B, March 20. Event description: free-entry neighborhood repair demonstration.” The email names Rin as organizer. It contains no other approval language. Receipt is undisputed.

## F2 — March 3 notice

Rin received a center email stating: “Events charging admission remain provisional until manager approval. Free-entry events are confirmed.” Rin read this notice on March 3. No manager approval for a fee-based Repair Circle event appears in the record. The notice says nothing about voluntary contributions.

## F3 — March 4 planning note

Rin's dated planning note states: “Ask for optional contributions to supplies. No one excluded for declining.” Rin supplied this note during intake and says this was the plan throughout. There is no statement from another organizer or would-be attendee confirming the entry arrangements. The note predates both expenses, but it is an organizer's account, not a center approval or a judicial finding.

## F4 — March 4 printer proof

A proof for the Repair Circle flyer says “Repair Circle — Room B — March 20 — $5 at door.” Rin approved printing the proof on March 4. The available record does not show the final distributed flyer or any later clarification of that wording. The phrase could support an inference of required payment; F3 and Rin's account support a competing inference of optional contributions. The record does not resolve what entrants would have been required to pay.

## F5 — March 5 printing payment

Rin paid 90 dollars for flyers specific to the confirmed event, room and date. The invoice and printer's written terms establish that the payment is nonrefundable, the flyers cannot be reused, and no credit is available. The expense was incurred and paid on March 5, before the cancellation. Do not substitute Moss's 80-dollar amount for Rin's 90 dollars.

## F6 — March 5 supply deposit and March 8 credit terms

Rin incurred and paid a 60-dollar deposit for event supplies on March 5. Following cancellation, the vendor denied a cash refund and offered a 60-dollar credit valid for one year, usable only on a future order of at least 100 dollars. The record contains no evidence of Rin's future supply needs, other usable purchases, transfer rights, or what portion of the credit Rin could practically use. No additional money has been spent to redeem the credit. The deposit's face amount is not automatically its nonrecoverable amount.

## F7 — March 7 cancellation and March 10 intake

The center canceled the reservation on March 7, writing: “Fee-based event not approved.” The cancellation itself is undisputed. Rin contests that characterization and says admission would have been free. The event has not taken place. Rin seeks reimbursement of the 90-dollar printing payment and 60-dollar supply deposit. Rin also asks whether time spent planning or expected contributions can be recovered. No court has ruled on any claim, and no other procedural event is supplied.

## Working convention

Attribute disputed assertions: “Rin reports” or “the planning note states.” Describe what documents say without converting an inference into an established fact. Separate a fact question, such as entry requirements, from a legal question, such as whether the communicated condition made reliance unreasonable. Cite F1–F7 after factual propositions. These record labels are sufficient for the course; they are not court docket or evidence designations.

references.title: Memo assignment and revision workbench
references.body:
## Assignment

Prepare a 900–1,100-word objective memorandum to a supervising attorney assessing Rin Patel's potential reimbursement under KCRA §§ 1–5 on the supplied record. Use the fictional trial-court forum and complete authority packet. Analyze reasonable reliance and the recoverable amount for each expense, and address the requested time and expected contributions under § 5. Use all three opinions where relevant. Do not research other legal claims. Explain that those claims fall outside the assignment without predicting their merits.

Write in your own document or notes. This course does not collect or automatically grade a memorandum. The quizzes check component skills. Use the rubric below for self-assessment; a human reviewer may apply it if available. Open the model memorandum after completing your first draft. A sound, supported prediction may differ from the model's degree of confidence.

## Deliverables

1. An issue-and-evidence matrix connecting each requirement to authority, favorable facts, adverse facts and missing information.
2. A first draft with a memo header, question presented, brief answer, statement of facts, discussion and conclusion.
3. A revised memorandum within the word range, including citations. Do not count the header or the separate revision log toward the word range.
4. A short revision log identifying at least three substantive changes. For each, give the old proposition, the revised proposition, the supporting source and why the change improves the analysis. Grammar-only changes do not satisfy these three entries.
5. A source audit with at least one verified proposition from each of §§ 1–5, Moss, Reed, Hale and F1–F7. Preserve paragraph or section locators. These audit entries are separate from the memorandum's word count.

## Suggested working sequence

Read the entire packet. Mark statutes, holdings and express limitations. Build the matrix before composing polished sentences. Outline by legal requirement and disputed question, not by a sequence of case names. Draft the discussion and facts, then write a brief answer that reflects the actual analysis. Revise the question presented if your first version omitted a central uncertainty. Keep the conclusion, discussion and brief answer consistent after each substantive revision.

## Matrix example

| Requirement or question | Legal source | Record | Analysis task |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Covered reservation | § 1; Reed ¶ 3 | F1 | Separate identification from reasonable reliance |
| Reliance on event approval | § 3; Moss ¶¶ 3–5; Reed ¶¶ 3–5 | F1–F4, F7 | Explain whether admission warning applied before payment |
| Printing loss | §§ 2, 4; Moss ¶ 4 | F5 | Establish timing and absence of retained value |
| Supply loss | § 4; Hale ¶¶ 2–5 | F6 | Examine practical credit value; avoid assumed total loss |
| Other requests | § 5 | F7 | Exclude time and expected contributions from this remedy |

This matrix is a starting structure. Add competing inferences and follow-up evidence. A cell containing only “good” or “bad” does not explain what a fact proves.

## Self-assessment rubric — 100 points

| Criterion | Points | Full-credit evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Issue and scope | 10 | Bounded reimbursement question, relevant uncertainty, packet-only scope |
| Rules and authorities | 20 | All statutory requirements; accurate Moss/Reed distinction; Hale reservation preserved |
| Application | 25 | Specific comparisons and reasons; each expense analyzed; no invented facts |
| Counteranalysis and prediction | 15 | Strong admission-fee objection; response tied to F3/F4; conditional credit assessment |
| Memo organization and tone | 10 | Consistent answer, useful headings, neutral facts, connected analysis |
| Citation and traceability | 10 | Each material legal and factual proposition has accurate support |
| Substantive revision | 10 | Three documented changes, source audit, unresolved questions honestly retained |

Award partial credit for work present but incomplete. A score is feedback about this exercise, not a university grade or credential. Revisit any unsupported legal proposition or invented fact even if the numerical total is high.

## Revision passes

**Structure:** Give each paragraph a one-line purpose. Move unrelated claims into separate analytical units. Check that each heading tells the reader the issue or supported prediction.

**Substance:** Trace every inference from evidence to rule to result. Add the strongest supported objection and answer it without changing the record. Separate confidence about printing from confidence about the credit.

**Sources:** Open each cited section or paragraph. Verify the actor, condition, date, amount and scope. Check quotations word for word. A nearby citation does not support every sentence in its paragraph automatically.

**Language:** Replace unsupported certainty, ambiguous pronouns and unnecessary nominalizations. Preserve legally important qualifiers. Read for factual neutrality and accessible sentences.

**Final comparison:** Compare the question presented, brief answer, discussion and conclusion. A new qualification about mandatory admission or credit usability must reach every section that otherwise overstates the answer.

references.title: Model objective memorandum and annotations
references.body:
Read after drafting. This is one supported approach to an unresolved record, not an exclusive answer or a prediction about real law. The memorandum uses only the fictional packet.

**To:** Supervising attorney  
**From:** Student analyst  
**Date:** March 10, teaching year  
**Re:** Rin Patel — canceled Repair Circle reservation

## Question presented

Under the Kestrel Community Room Act, can Rin recover preparation expenses after the center canceled an identified, confirmed event, where a prepayment notice made fee-based events conditional on approval, the entry-payment arrangements are disputed, and one vendor offered a restricted credit?

## Brief answer

Rin has a plausible claim for the 90-dollar printing expense, but recovery depends on establishing reasonable reliance. If entry was genuinely free, the express confirmation and notice preserving free-entry approval support recovery. The approved flyer proof's “$5 at door” language creates a substantial contrary inference that the event required approval. The additional 60-dollar supply claim depends on practical credit value as well as reasonable reliance. Its amount cannot be fixed from this record. Time and expected contributions are outside the Act's preparation-expense remedy. KCRA §§ 2–5.

## Statement of facts

On March 2, the center confirmed Repair Circle for Room B on March 20, identifying it as a free-entry demonstration. On March 3, Rin received and read a notice requiring manager approval for events charging admission while confirming free-entry events. F1–F2. Rin's March 4 note described optional contributions and no exclusion for nonpayment. A printer proof approved that day stated “$5 at door”; the final distributed wording and entry arrangements are unavailable. F3–F4. Rin paid 90 dollars for nonrefundable, unusable event-specific flyers and a 60-dollar supply deposit on March 5. F5–F6. The center canceled March 7, characterizing the event as fee-based and unapproved. Rin disputes that characterization. After cancellation, the supply vendor offered a one-year credit requiring a future order of at least 100 dollars. The record does not establish whether Rin could use its value. F6–F7.

## Discussion

The Act requires a covered reservation, center cancellation, reasonable reliance and a nonrecoverable preparation expense paid before cancellation. KCRA § 2. The named event, room and date satisfy § 1; the center canceled, and both payments preceded cancellation. F1, F5–F7. Those circumstances do not themselves resolve reliance or retained value. Reed ¶ 3. The principal questions are whether the admission condition applied when Rin paid and how much of each payment remains unrecoverable.

### I. Reasonable reliance turns on the event's entry arrangements

Rin's reliance is supportable if the planned event remained free-entry, but the contrary evidence prevents an unconditional prediction. Section 3 considers confirmation specificity, relevant prepayment warnings and the expense's connection to the event. In Moss, a general room-change footer did not condition event approval; the court allowed event-specific printing costs. Moss ¶¶ 1, 3–4. In Reed, an acknowledged safety-approval condition remained unsatisfied before payment. The court denied reimbursement despite a writing headed “Reservation.” Reed ¶¶ 1, 3–4. The decisions distinguish a notice's effect on event approval, rather than treating every warning alike.

Rin's confirmation specifically identified a free-entry event, and the later notice expressly preserved confirmation for that category. F1–F2. If contributions were optional as the planning note states, the manager-approval condition may not have applied. F3. That would make the booking's commitment closer to Moss's approved event than Reed's expressly conditional event. The flyers' event, room and date also connect that expense to the confirmed reservation. F5; KCRA § 3. The confirmation is therefore meaningful support, although it is not conclusive proof of reasonable reliance.

The center has a substantial response: the approved proof's “$5 at door” wording suggests an admission charge, and Rin had read the approval notice before paying. F2, F4. If payment was required for entry, Reed strongly supports finding reliance unreasonable because the applicable condition remained unsatisfied. No such approval appears in the record. F2; Reed ¶¶ 3–5. Rin can point to the earlier optional-contribution note, but that account does not establish what entrants would actually have been required to pay. F3–F4. Conversely, the center's cancellation label does not establish the disputed arrangement by itself. F7. The final publicity and instructions to other organizers could materially strengthen one account. On the present record, the printing claim is plausible but exposed to this factual dispute.

### II. Printing has an established loss; the supply credit needs valuation

If reasonable reliance is established, the 90-dollar printing expense appears recoverable. Section 4 excludes recoverable value, while allowing an identifiable nonrecoverable portion. The printing terms establish no refund, reuse or credit, and payment preceded cancellation. F5. These features resemble the event-specific flyers reimbursed in Moss and the separate labels allowed in Hale. Moss ¶ 4; Hale ¶¶ 2, 4. Their different amounts do not change why the expenses qualify. No additional uncertainty about retained printing value appears in this record.

The supply deposit cannot simply be added as another 60-dollar loss. Hale denied a supply claim where an unrestricted credit's full value was usable for planned purchases, even though the vendor denied a cash refund. Hale ¶¶ 2–3. Rin likewise has a credit, but it expires in one year and requires an order of at least 100 dollars. F6. Those limits differ from Hale's fully usable credit, and Hale expressly left restricted credits unresolved. Hale ¶ 5. The restrictions support investigating reduced usable value; they do not prove that all value is lost. Evidence of future supply needs, alternative purchases and transfer rights would help determine the nonrecoverable portion under § 4. Without that evidence, neither zero loss nor a full 60-dollar loss is established.

## Conclusion

The strongest quantified claim is the 90-dollar printing expense, conditional on reasonable reliance. Obtain final publicity and entry instructions to assess whether admission required payment. Investigate practical use of the supply credit before assigning a recoverable amount. Evaluate that expense separately rather than promising a 150-dollar award. Rin's planning time and anticipated contributions are excluded from this remedy; possible claims under other law remain outside this assignment. KCRA § 5; F7.

## Annotations outside the memorandum

The memo separates law, record and prediction. It does not silently accept either the client's preferred label or the center's cancellation label. It explains the reason Moss and Reed differ, rather than counting favorable and adverse cases. Its Hale comparison preserves the court's reserved issue. Its conclusion identifies evidence that could change the answer.

A stronger or weaker overall prediction can earn full rubric credit if supported and calibrated to this record. An unconditional reimbursement prediction cannot be justified merely by the existence of a confirmation or a nonrefundable payment. A categorical denial based only on the existence of any credit also misstates § 4 and Hale.
